# 1\. Document Purpose

This test plan explains how we will test the Marco Polo Smart RF Asset Recovery System without overcomplicating it. The goal is to prove that a Hider tag can share its location over LoRa and, when GPS is not available, switch into a simple Marco Polo recovery mode so the Seeker can move toward it.

This is a draft. It will change as the T-Beam hardware arrives and as the team learns what actually works during testing.

# 2\. System Under Test

The planned end-state system has two main parts:

* Hider: an asset tag with GPS, LoRa, battery power, and basic sensor support. It sends location and status packets.  
* Seeker: a LoRa receiver device that receives Hider packets, shows the last known location, and helps the user search.  
* TinyML kit: used for sensor/event work if time allows, such as movement, vibration, orientation, or disturbance detection.

The core project story is simple: GPS when it works, Marco Polo mode when it does not.

# 3\. What We Are Testing

In scope for the main test plan:

* Basic LoRa packet sending and receiving.  
* GPS acquisition on the Hider.  
* GPS coordinates sent from Hider to Seeker over LoRa.  
* Seeker display/logging of tag ID, mode, packet count, and location.  
* GPS-lost mode using a switch, software flag, or safe simulation.  
* Marco Polo chirp packets for recovery mode.  
* Basic hotter/colder search behavior using RSSI if available, or packet rate / packet age if RSSI is not available.  
* Simple logs and screenshots for final report evidence.

Out of scope for this draft:

* Production security/encryption.  
* Long-term battery endurance testing.  
* Weatherproofing or rugged enclosure validation.  
* Large-scale multi-tag testing.  
* Robot recovery as a required test. Robot recovery is a stretch goal only.

# 4\. Simple Test Strategy

The plan is to test one layer at a time so we do not get stuck debugging everything at once.

1. Prove LoRa communication with simple test packets.  
2. Add GPS and confirm the Hider gets valid coordinates outdoors.  
3. Send GPS coordinates over LoRa and confirm the Seeker receives the same data.  
4. Add GPS-lost mode and confirm the Hider sends last known GPS plus recovery chirps.  
5. Test basic Marco Polo recovery by moving the Seeker closer/farther and logging what changes.  
6. Save enough data to support a short, honest analysis in the final report.

# 5\. General Pass Criteria

* The Hider powers on and sends packets without repeated crashes or resets.  
* The Seeker receives readable Hider packets in a usable format.  
* GPS lock is acquired outdoors or under clear-sky conditions. Near-window testing can be recorded, but it should not be a strict pass/fail condition.  
* GPS packets include tag ID, mode, latitude, longitude, and packet count or timestamp.  
* In short-range testing, at least 90% of test packets should be received. Higher is better, but 90% is acceptable for the prototype.  
* When GPS is unavailable or disabled, the Hider sends GPS\_LOST or MARCO\_POLO status with the last known location.  
* The Seeker shows recovery-useful trend data, such as RSSI if available, packet rate, packet age, packet success, or distance trend.  
* Logs/screenshots are saved well enough that another teammate can understand what happened.

# 6\. Test Cases

## TC-01: LoRa Link Check

Objective: Confirm that the Hider can send simple LoRa packets and the Seeker can receive them.

Basic steps:

* Power both devices with antennas attached.  
* Send a test packet every 2 seconds, such as HIDER01,TEST,PKT=1.  
* Run for at least 30 packets.  
* Record sent count, received count, and any weird behavior.

Pass criteria:

* Seeker receives readable packets.  
* Packet numbers are readable and mostly in order.

## TC-02: GPS Acquisition

Objective: Confirm that the Hider can get a valid GPS fix.

Basic steps:

* Place the Hider outdoors or under clear sky.  
* Power it on and wait for GPS fix.  
* Record time to first valid fix, coordinates, and satellites if available.

Pass criteria:

* Latitude and longitude are valid and not default/zero values.  
* Coordinates roughly match the test area.

## TC-03: GPS Over LoRa

Objective: Confirm that the Hider can send GPS location packets over LoRa and the Seeker can read them.

Basic steps:

* Get valid GPS on the Hider.  
* Start GPS\_OK LoRa packets.  
* Confirm Seeker receives tag ID, mode, latitude, longitude, and packet count.

Pass criteria:

* Seeker receives GPS\_OK packets.  
* Received coordinates match what the Hider sent.

## TC-04: Seeker Display and Logging

Objective: Confirm that the Seeker output is useful for the demo and final report.

Basic steps:

* Show received data in Serial Monitor, dashboard, map, or Raspberry Pi display.  
* Log packets to CSV, JSON, text, or database.  
* Save one sample log and one screenshot.

Pass criteria:

* A user can identify the Hider, mode, location, and packet count.  
* A basic log is saved.  
* Display/logging does not crash during a short test.

## TC-05: GPS-Lost / No GPS Mode

Objective: Confirm that the Hider can simulate or detect GPS loss and keep sending useful recovery packets.

Basic steps:

* Start with a valid GPS fix.  
* Trigger GPS-lost mode using a switch, software flag, safe GPS blocking, or simulation.  
* Confirm Hider changes from GPS\_OK to GPS\_LOST or MARCO\_POLO.  
* Confirm last known GPS is preserved.

Pass criteria:

* Mode change is visible in the logs.  
* Last known location is not erased or replaced with bad data.  
* System keeps running after mode change.

## TC-06: Marco Polo Recovery Test

Objective: Confirm that the Seeker can use RF behavior to help move toward the Hider.

Basic steps:

* Place the Hider in a fixed hidden location.  
* Move the Seeker through at least three positions.  
* At each position, record RSSI if available, or packet rate, packet age, packet success, and distance if GPS is available.  
* Classify each move as hotter, colder, or unclear.

Pass criteria:

* The Seeker records a useful trend across positions.  
* At least two movement decisions are correctly labeled hotter/colder in a controlled test.  
* If the trend is unclear, the limitation is documented honestly.

## TC-07: End-to-End Demo Test

Objective: Show the full project story in one short demo.

Basic steps:

* Start in GPS\_OK mode and show location sharing.  
* Switch to GPS\_LOST / MARCO\_POLO mode.  
* Show chirp/recovery packets being received.  
* Move the Seeker and show search trend data.  
* Save screenshots, logs, and video if available.

Pass criteria:

* Demo shows GPS sharing.  
* Demo shows GPS-lost recovery mode.  
* Evidence is good enough for the final report/presentation.

# 7\. Data to Save

* Date/time and tester.  
* Hardware used.  
* Tag ID and packet number.  
* Mode: TEST, GPS\_OK, GPS\_LOST, or MARCO\_POLO.  
* Latitude/longitude when available.  
* Last known latitude/longitude when GPS is lost.  
* Packets sent and packets received.  
* RSSI if the hardware provides it. If not, use packet rate, packet age, and packet success.  
* Notes on distance, walls, location, and movement.  
* Screenshots, photos, serial logs, and optional video.

# 8\. Risks and Simple Backups

* GPS may not lock indoors. Backup: test GPS outdoors and use GPS-lost simulation for indoor tests.  
* LoRa packets may fail due to wiring or settings. Backup: start with plain text packets before GPS data.  
* RSSI may be unavailable or too noisy. Backup: use packet success, packet rate, packet age, or a future receiver that exposes RSSI.  
* Scope may grow too much. Backup: protect the basic demo first and keep robot recovery as stretch only.  
* TinyML may take longer than expected. Backup: collect sensor data now and treat TinyML classification as a later layer if needed.

# 9\. Go / No-Go Decision

Each test gets one of three results:

* GO: works well enough to move forward.  
* CONDITIONAL: mostly works, but needs a fix or note.  
* NO-GO: blocks the next step and must be fixed first.

For the final demo, the project should show GPS location sharing, GPS-lost or simulated GPS-lost behavior, Marco Polo recovery packets, and at least one simple data analysis result from the logs.
